explanation: Its branches and roots join the nine worlds. In the Prose Edda an eagle perches at the top, a dragon gnaws a root, and a squirrel carries insults between them.

claims.text: In Norse myth, Yggdrasil is an immense ash tree.
Yggdrasil is not the rainbow bridge (Bifröst), the hall of warriors (Valhalla) or the sea serpent (Jörmungandr).
In Norse myth, Yggdrasil's branches and roots link the nine worlds.
In the Prose Edda, an eagle sits at the top of Yggdrasil, the dragon Níðhöggr gnaws at a root, and the squirrel Ratatoskr carries insults between them.

evidence.restatement: Yggdrasil is the great ash tree at the centre of the Norse cosmos.
The rainbow bridge is Bifröst, the hall of slain warriors is Valhalla and the sea serpent is Jörmungandr.
The Eddic poems speak of nine worlds, and standard accounts describe Yggdrasil as the tree that links them.

claimResults.note: High-risk (number), knowledge only: no pinned dataset covers it and no web search could run (the shared web-search budget was used up), so it still needs dataset or web evidence before acceptance (§9.9 rule 3).

evidence.restatement: Gylfaginning in Snorri's Prose Edda puts an eagle in the tree's branches and Níðhöggr at a root, with the squirrel Ratatoskr carrying spiteful words between them.
Norse sources (Völuspá, the Prose Edda) describe Yggdrasil as a huge ash tree at the centre of the cosmos.

claimResults.note: Rival test: some scholars have argued for a yew, but the sources say ash (askr).

evidence.restatement: Bifröst is the rainbow bridge, Valhalla the hall of slain warriors and Jörmungandr the world serpent; none of them is Yggdrasil.
Reference works say the nine worlds lie around or within Yggdrasil, but I cannot confirm that the sources say its branches and roots join or link them.

claimResults.note: checker_doubt c3: no search was possible (budget exhausted). In the Prose Edda the tree has three roots (the gods' well, Mimir's well, Hvergelmir) and branches over all the world; the nine worlds are named in Völuspá. "Link the nine worlds" looks like a modern gloss.

evidence.restatement: In the Prose Edda (Gylfaginning) an eagle sits in the top of the tree, the dragon Níðhöggr gnaws at a root and the squirrel Ratatoskr runs between them carrying insulting words.

issues.note: checker_doubt c3: the explanation says the tree's branches and roots "join" the nine worlds. Sources support "the nine worlds lie around or within the tree"; "join" is a modern gloss, and I found no way to check it without a search. Reword to what the sources state (for example "its roots reach three wells") or evidence the linking claim with a Tier A or B source.
